problemSolved: Default LLM output for 'build a UI' regresses to safe, generic templates because there is no evaluative pressure.
mechanism: Opens by assigning the model a persona ('design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's') plus a fictional client who already rejected templated proposals.
whyItWorks: Persona + adversarial backstory changes the implicit reward function the model optimizes for mid-generation: it now self-evaluates against 'would this be mistaken for someone else's work' rather than 'does this look like a finished website.' This is a context-shaping move, not a content rule.
requiredContext: none — self-contained sentence, no external state
outputImpact: Shifts the model's internal acceptance bar before a single design decision is made; everything downstream inherits the stricter bar.
failureModes: Persona alone does not guarantee follow-through without the later self-critique step (see self-critique-loop) — a model can adopt the persona's tone in prose while still shipping a template layout.
conflicts: None found in this source; complements structural rules rather than competing.
testMethod: Asserted only — no mechanism in this package checks whether the persona actually changed the output. Blind-test result (59 vs 40) is external evidence the whole package works, not proof this line specifically matters.
sitesmithForm: Open the direction-setting step of SiteSmith with an equivalent persona + adversarial-client framing sentence, kept to 1-2 sentences so it doesn't crowd out the subject-grounding step that must follow.

problemSolved: Vague or content-free briefs are the single biggest cause of generic output — the model has nothing specific to differentiate against.
mechanism: If the brief doesn't pin down the subject, the model is instructed to invent one itself: 'name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice.' It is explicitly told to mine its own memory of the user's stated preferences or prior work as a hint, and to draw distinctive choices from 'the subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular.'
whyItWorks: This is the direct antidote to house-style convergence: instead of falling back to a fixed palette/layout when the brief is thin, the model is forced to manufacture domain-specific texture (a tannery's tools, a leatherworker's vocabulary) that mechanically cannot be the same across two different subjects.
requiredContext: optionally prior memory/preferences about the user
outputImpact: This is the single mechanism most directly responsible for avoiding the 'three sites converge on five moves' failure documented in our own benchmark decision.
failureModes: If the model's 'concrete subject' choice is itself generic (e.g. always picking a coffee shop when unconstrained), grounding does not help — the instruction constrains form, not choice of subject.
No verification that the invented subject was actually used throughout the build.
conflicts: None internal. External: this is exactly the mechanism our C-no-house-style finding says must not be short-circuited by a template.
sitesmithForm: Make subject-grounding a mandatory, explicit step in SiteSmith's direction phase: require the model to state subject + audience + page job as text output before any token system is proposed, sourced from brief content and, if thin, invented and flagged as invented.

problemSolved: Hero sections default to 'big number + small label + gradient accent' regardless of subject, because that pattern is heavily represented in training data.
mechanism: States the hero must be 'a thesis' — the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form fits (headline, image, animation, live demo, interactive moment) — and explicitly names the stat-block pattern as 'the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.'
whyItWorks: Naming the default pattern out loud and demoting it to 'last resort, justify it' converts an unconscious default into a conscious, effortful choice — the model has to argue for the cliché rather than reach for it by inertia.
requiredContext: subject grounding must already exist (depends on subject-grounding-mandate)
outputImpact: High-leverage single line: the hero is the first thing a viewer and a blind judge see, so this is disproportionately responsible for a 'this looks different' first impression.
failureModes: Still permits the stat-block pattern when 'truly best' — a model that rationalizes weakly could use this as license to keep the default anyway.
sitesmithForm: Keep a short list of 2-3 named 'default hero patterns to justify before using' (stat block, gradient-hero-with-CTA, carousel) as an explicit check in the plan-review step, not as banned patterns — as patterns requiring justification.

problemSolved: Type pairing defaults to 'the same families you would reach for on any other project' — a template signature even when colors and layout differ.
mechanism: Instructs deliberate display/body pairing specific to the brief, a clear type scale with intentional weights/widths/spacing, and frames type treatment as 'a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle.'
whyItWorks: Elevates typography from an implementation detail (pick a Google Font pair) to a design decision with the same weight as color — this is a reframing, not a rule, so it transfers to any subject without needing a font database.
outputImpact: Directly targets one of the 'five convergent moves' risk areas — font choice is one of the most visually obvious tells of house style.
failureModes: No concrete guidance on how to source non-default font pairs — a model without strong type knowledge may still reach for the same 3-4 'safe' pairings it always uses, just with more confidence.
sitesmithForm: Fold into the token-system step: require the plan to name the display/body/utility typefaces and state, in one clause, why this pairing fits this subject (not just 'looks nice').

problemSolved: Structural devices (numbered steps 01/02/03, eyebrows, dividers) get applied decoratively regardless of whether the content is actually sequential — a widely recognized 'AI template' tell.
mechanism: States structural devices 'should encode something true about the content, not decorate it,' and explicitly calls out numbered markers as appropriate 'only if the content actually is a sequence,' instructing the model to question the choice before using it.
whyItWorks: This is a targeted anti-pattern callout: it names the specific tell (numbered markers) that judges and users recognize as generic, and ties its legitimacy to a testable condition (is this actually ordered content?) rather than banning it outright.
requiredContext: content/information architecture of the specific page
outputImpact: Medium — removes one of the most visually obvious 'AI-generated' signals when content isn't actually sequential.
failureModes: Only covers one structural device (numbering) by name; does not generalize to other decorative structural tells (e.g. three-column feature grids used regardless of whether there are three natural groupings).
sitesmithForm: Generalize the underlying test ('does this structural device encode something true about the content?') as a reusable self-check applied to any structural device, not just numbering, during the plan-review step.

problemSolved: Motion/animation is either absent (flat, static default) or scattered (hover effects added everywhere with no orchestration) — both read as generic or noisy.
mechanism: Frames motion as a choice tied to the subject ('think about where and if animation can serve the subject'), prefers one orchestrated moment over scattered effects, and explicitly warns that 'extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.'
whyItWorks: Directly counters a known overcorrection: models that learn 'add animation to seem polished' tend to sprinkle micro-interactions everywhere. Naming that this itself reads as AI-generated flips the incentive.
requiredContext: subject grounding, to know what an 'orchestrated moment' would even be for this subject
outputImpact: Medium — mostly affects perceived craft and restraint rather than first-impression differentiation.
failureModes: No verification a model actually implements the chosen motion correctly (respecting reduced-motion, performance) — that's covered separately in the quality-floor mechanism.
sitesmithForm: Keep as a one-line principle in the direction step: 'pick zero or one orchestrated motion moment tied to the subject; do not default to scattered hover effects.'

problemSolved: The model has no internal reference for what 'generic AI design' currently looks like, so it can't recognize when its own output matches the pattern.
mechanism: Names three specific, currently-observed AI-design clusters verbatim (cream #F4F1EA + serif + terracotta; near-black + single acid/vermilion accent; broadsheet hairline-rule newspaper layout) and instructs the model to check its own plan against these before building, while also stating the brief's explicit request always wins even if it asks for one of these looks.
whyItWorks: This is the most concrete, checkable anti-house-style device in the whole file: a fuzzy 'be original' instruction gives the model nothing to test against; naming three actual patterns turns self-critique into a real diff-against-known-defaults instead of vague self-congratulation.
requiredContext: none — self-contained, but factually time-bound (these are 2025-era observed clusters, will go stale)
outputImpact: High — this is very plausibly the single biggest contributor to the 59-vs-40 result, because it's the only mechanism that gives the model a concrete self-test for house-style convergence rather than a mood.
failureModes: Hard-coded list will age: new clichés emerge, and this list cannot update itself (no mechanism to refresh it, since there's no script, just static prose committed once).

Only catches the three named patterns — a model could still converge on a fourth, unnamed pattern (which is arguably what happened to the old SiteSmith house style, per our own benchmark-decision memory).
conflicts: This is in tension with fixed 'brand design system' style guides some teams want to enforce — this mechanism assumes freedom to deviate, so it cannot coexist with a hard brand-lock requirement without a carve-out (which the source itself provides: 'brief's own words always win').
testMethod: Asserted only, but externally corroborated: this is the mechanism most directly targeted by the C-no-house-style finding from our own three-site convergence test.
sitesmithForm: Carry an explicit, maintained list of currently-observed generic patterns (updated periodically, not frozen) as a mandatory self-check before the build step — this is the highest-value single mechanism to reproduce, and it must be a living list, not copied verbatim once and left stale.

problemSolved: An anti-cliché rule could wrongly override an explicit client request that happens to match a named cliché.
mechanism: A single clause: 'Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks.'
whyItWorks: Prevents the anti-house-style instruction from becoming its own rigid rule that fights the actual brief — it scopes the anti-cliché pressure to only the axes the brief left open.
requiredContext: the brief text, to know what's pinned down vs. free
outputImpact: Low frequency but high consequence when triggered — prevents a specific class of bad override.
failureModes: Requires the model to correctly classify 'pinned down' vs 'free' — an ambiguous brief could be misread either way with no check.
sitesmithForm: Keep this override explicit and adjacent to any anti-cliché list we adopt, so the two clauses are read together, not the cliché-list alone.

problemSolved: Jumping straight to code causes design decisions to be made ad hoc and inconsistently, and makes it hard to critique the direction before cost is sunk in implementation.
mechanism: Requires a compact, named token system produced in a first pass, before code: color (4-6 named hex values), type (2+ typefaces by role), layout (prose + ASCII wireframe concept), and signature (the one unique memorable element).
whyItWorks: Externalizing the decision as a short, structured artifact makes it reviewable — both by the self-critique step that follows and, in principle, by a human — before the much larger and harder-to-critique step of writing code.
requiredContext: no external tool needed — this is model-authored prose/ASCII, not a generated file
outputImpact: High — this is the artifact the self-critique step operates on; without it, 'review the plan' has nothing concrete to review.
failureModes: ASCII wireframes are a weak substitute for real layout tools and can hide problems (overlap, overflow) that only show up once real CSS is written.

No mechanism requires the token system to be shown to the user before building (the source explicitly says the opposite: 'only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence' — see private-reasoning-before-reveal), so a bad plan can still ship unseen if the self-critique step is weak.
sitesmithForm: Reuse the four-part token system (color/type/layout/signature) verbatim as SiteSmith's direction-phase output contract — it is concrete, cheap, and gives the self-critique step something to bite on.

problemSolved: A model's first idea is disproportionately likely to be its most statistically common (i.e. generic) idea; nothing forces reconsideration before commitment.
mechanism: After the plan is drafted, the model is told to review it against the brief and against 'the generic default you would produce for any similar page' by explicitly imagining a similar prompt and checking if it converges to the same place, then revise and state what changed and why. Only after this passes does code get written.
whyItWorks: This is a single self-critique iteration, same model, no external critic, no adversarial second model. It works (per the blind-test result) because it forces an explicit counterfactual comparison ('would a similar brief produce the same plan?') rather than a vague 'is this good' check — see LOOPS.md for full analysis of iteration count and stop condition.
requiredContext: the draft token system from two-pass-token-system
the named-cliche-calibration list as a concrete comparison target
outputImpact: This is very likely the second-highest-leverage mechanism after named-cliche-calibration — it's the enforcement step, not just the standard.
failureModes: Single iteration, self-graded — no external verification the revision actually improved anything (see LOOPS.md and TESTING.md).
Can be skipped or rushed under time/token pressure since nothing external gates it — it's a norm, not a checkpoint enforced by tooling.
testMethod: Asserted only — no rubric, no second model, no measurable pass/fail threshold given in the source.
sitesmithForm: Keep as a mandatory single self-critique pass in SiteSmith's direction phase, explicitly against the living cliché list; consider (as an adaptation, not present in the source) logging the 'what I changed and why' note so it's auditable rather than silent.

problemSolved: A narrow, concrete implementation bug class: type-based selectors (`.section`) and element-based selectors (`.cta`) silently canceling each other out, especially in padding/margin between sections.
mechanism: A single warning sentence naming the specific failure pattern.
whyItWorks: This is not a creative-reasoning mechanism at all — it's a narrow implementation tip. It works simply because it's specific and names a real, recurring bug class rather than a vague 'write good CSS' instruction.
outputImpact: Low — affects code correctness, not creative differentiation. Orthogonal to the C-no-mechanical-creativity / C-no-house-style axes.
failureModes: Too narrow to matter much on its own; only useful if the model is actually writing raw CSS with class-based cascades (framework-dependent, e.g. less relevant under Tailwind/utility-first CSS).
conflicts: Stack-dependent: irrelevant or even actively unhelpful noise if the build target is a utility-CSS framework rather than hand-rolled cascading classes.
sitesmithForm: Not a priority mechanism to port; if kept, gate it behind stack detection (only surface when hand-written CSS with class+element selectors is actually in play) rather than always-on.

problemSolved: Showing half-formed ideas to the user/judge too early anchors the conversation on a weak first draft and wastes the user's attention on iteration that could have happened silently.
mechanism: 'Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.'
whyItWorks: Pushes the brainstorm-critique cycle into the model's private reasoning trace rather than the visible conversation, so the visible output is already past at least one round of self-rejection.
requiredContext: a runtime that supports private/extended thinking distinct from the final visible response
outputImpact: Medium — improves perceived output quality by hiding the messy intermediate steps, but has no effect if the runtime has no private-reasoning channel (would then just mean 'think it through before typing,' which is weaker but still directionally useful).
failureModes: Assumes a runtime feature (extended/private thinking) that may not exist in every deployment context — a plain single-pass completion API has no separate private channel, so this degrades to a soft suggestion.
conflicts: Runtime-dependent: valuable when the calling agent has a visible/hidden reasoning split (as Claude Code does); close to a no-op instruction in runtimes without one.
sitesmithForm: Keep the instruction but frame it runtime-agnostically: 'iterate on the plan before presenting it,' relying on whatever privacy the host runtime offers rather than assuming a specific thinking-channel feature.

problemSolved: Undisciplined creativity spreads boldness evenly across a page, which reads as busy/unfocused rather than as a deliberate design statement; conversely, over-restraint can be its own failure to take a risk.
mechanism: 'Spend your boldness in one place' — the signature element (identified earlier in the token system) is the one memorable thing; everything else is quiet and disciplined. Explicitly also warns the opposite failure: 'Not taking a risk can be a risk itself.' Paired with a concrete quality floor (responsive to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected) that must be met without being called out ('build to a quality floor without announcing it').
whyItWorks: Concentrating risk in one deliberately chosen element, while holding everything else to a disciplined baseline, is what makes a design read as intentional rather than chaotic or timid — it operationalizes 'elegance' as a resource-allocation rule rather than a vague aesthetic goal.
requiredContext: the signature element named in the token system (two-pass-token-system)
outputImpact: High for perceived craft and cohesion; this is the mechanism that keeps 'take one real aesthetic risk' (SKILL.md:9) from producing a scattered, over-decorated result.
failureModes: No accessibility testing tool is provided to confirm the quality floor (keyboard focus, reduced motion, responsiveness) was actually met — it's an assertion, not a gate (see TESTING.md).
Screenshot self-critique is suggested ('taking screenshots if your environment supports it') but not required or tooled — degrades silently in environments without screenshot capability.
testMethod: Asserted only for the aesthetic claim; the quality-floor items (keyboard focus, reduced motion, responsive) are checkable with real tools but the source does not name or require any.
sitesmithForm: Keep the resource-allocation framing (signature element gets the risk budget, everything else is disciplined) as an explicit rule in SiteSmith's build phase, and pair it with SiteSmith's own actual verification gate (scripts/verify.mjs-equivalent) rather than leaving the quality floor as an assertion.

problemSolved: Placeholder or generic copy ('Submit', 'Something went wrong', feature-speak like 'webhook config') is itself a strong signal of templated, unconsidered design, even when visuals are original.
mechanism: A dedicated section treats words as 'design material, not decoration': write from the end user's perspective using vocabulary for what people control (not system internals), default to active voice with persistent verb identity across a flow (a 'Publish' button produces a 'Published' toast), treat errors/empty-states as directional moments in the interface's voice, and keep register conversational and tuned to brand/audience.
whyItWorks: This generalizes the anti-genericism principle from visuals to language — the same 'don't default to the safe template' pressure applied to a different medium (words), using concrete, checkable rules (active voice, persistent verb identity, no system-internals vocabulary) rather than a vague 'write good copy' instruction.
requiredContext: the actual content/flow of the interface being designed (what actions exist, what they're called)
outputImpact: Medium-high — generic placeholder copy is one of the most common tells that a design brief wasn't really considered end to end; this closes that gap even when the brief provided no real content.
failureModes: No test given for tone appropriateness — 'conversational and tuned' is asserted, not measured.

Persistent verb identity across a flow ('Publish' -> 'Published') requires the model to track state across multiple UI surfaces in one build; nothing in the source verifies this consistency was kept, especially on longer builds.
sitesmithForm: Port the concrete rules (active voice default, persistent verb identity end-to-end, user-facing vocabulary not system vocabulary, error/empty states written in interface voice) as an explicit copy checklist alongside the visual token system, so copy gets the same brainstorm-critique treatment as color/type/layout.
